newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FORECAST-Iberia spread on bunds seen near 100 bps.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Iberia spread on bunds seen near 100 bps.

text.p: The spread between Spanish and Portuguese 10-year cash bonds and German Bunds should stick next week between 95 and 105 basis points -- the short-term boundary for optimism and pessimism about the two countries' EMU chances, traders said.

The likelihood that Spain's January inflation numbers will be better than Portugal's could help Bonos -- Spanish bonds -- to outperform the Portuguese OT at the shorter end of the yield curve up to three years, they added.
"This week should be calmer. The (spread of the) 10-year Bonos and OT could oscillate between 95 and 105 basis points," said analyst Valentin Fernandez of Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
The spread between 10-year Spanish and Portuguese bonds and Bunds stood at 103 and 102 basis points respectively on Friday against all-time lows of 83 and 80 basis points at the end of January.

"After the crisis over the possible non-entry of the peripheral markets into monetary union, Iberia has a top of 95 basis points and a bottom of 105 basis points," said an analyst with the London bank.
Mario Vigario of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell (DMG) saw the spread between 100 and 105 basis points.

"At the beginning of the week, the (Spanish) spread over the Bund could be around 100 basis points and then rally to 95 on expectations for a good CPI (consumer price index) number," said Vicente Fernandez.

Vigario said that Portugal was well-supported at a zero spread to the Spanish market so if Spain rose, Portugal would go up too, with the spread between the two Iberian markets moving between zero and a discount of five basis points.

But with the Spanish year-on-year inflation rate likely to ease from December's 3.2 percent and the Portuguese rate possibly rising from 3.3 percent -- albeit for purely statistical reasons -- the shorter end of the Spanish curve was likely to perform better than Portugal.

"With a good inflation number, the Bank of Spain can lower rates, even as early as Friday. We even think it could cut 50 basis points off the repo to 5.50 percent," said Bank of America analyst in Madrid Henrik Lumholdt.
"The peseta has already begun to recover slowly and I believe that it is going to strengthen. It is enough for the Bank of Spain," he said.
But the Bank of Portugal was unlikely to touch its rates until it was certain both inflation and the escudo were calm, analysts in Lisbon said.
The Spanish CPI is expected on February 13 while Portugal will issue its numbers between February 14 and 17.
"If the expectation is that the Bank of Spain will cut rates and the Bank of Portugal will not, the Bonos up to three years will gain against the OT," said Fernandez.
The spread between the January 1999 OT and the April 1999 Bono is eight basis points.
"Nevertheless, the widening of the spread will be nothing dramatic because the rise in the CPI in Portugal is a mechanical one and inflation is going to fall later on," said one London analyst.
"It is not a structural divergence (between Portugal and Spain)," said Armindo Escalda of Banco Santander de Negocios Portugal.
With a good inflation number, the Spanish yield curve was likely to steepen, analysts said.
"The curve flattened and could steepen again. The spread between the 10 years and the two years could be around 135 basis points by the end of next year," said Lumholdt.
The spread is currently 128 basis points.
--Lisbon bureau 3511-3150035
